```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(bayesDP)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center", dpi = 150)
```

# Purpose and current limitations

`bdpsurvival()` uses piecewise constant hazards for right-censored outcomes. In one arm, the estimand is survival probability at a specified time. With two arms, the reported effect is an approximate common log hazard ratio, treatment relative to control.

Three limitations remain under investigation: the default Monte Carlo weight calculation ([issue 16](https://github.com/graemeleehickey/bayesDP/issues/16)), the baseline-prior contribution during historical augmentation ([issue 17](https://github.com/graemeleehickey/bayesDP/issues/17)), and participant counts/risk sets in `summary()` ([issue 18](https://github.com/graemeleehickey/bayesDP/issues/18)). These examples use `method = "fixed"`, describe the implemented prior update, and calculate tables directly from posterior draws. They illustrate current behaviour; they do not validate the unresolved procedures for trial design.

See the [borrowing overview](borrowing.html) for weighting choices and interpretation. The function default is `method = "mc"`, so the explicit method argument matters.

# Data and follow-up

Supply current and historical data frames with compatible columns. Use `Surv(time, status) ~ 1` for a one-arm analysis, or `Surv(time, status) ~ treatment` for two arms. Code `status = 1` for an event and `status = 0` for right censoring; `time` is the observed event or censoring time. For two arms, code `treatment = 1` and control as 0, and provide both arms in both studies for the examples below. Additional covariate adjustment is not implemented.

Choose a time unit, clinically relevant survival horizon, and interval boundaries. `breaks` contains positive internal cutpoints, without zero or infinity. The final interval extends beyond the last cutpoint. By default the cutpoints are the pooled observed-time 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentiles; these are quantiles of event-or-censoring times, not estimated survival quantiles. The examples prespecify cutpoints and the horizon.

# One-arm example with censoring

We simulate event times with mean 10 months for 60 current participants and mean 11 months for 100 historical participants. Independent censoring times have mean 18 months, with additional administrative censoring at 18 months. The observed time is the minimum of event and censoring times.

```{r censored-data}
simulate_followup <- function(n, mean_event, mean_censor, horizon) {
  event_time <- rexp(n, rate = 1 / mean_event)
  censor_time <- pmin(rexp(n, rate = 1 / mean_censor), horizon)
  data.frame(time = pmin(event_time, censor_time),
    status = as.integer(event_time <= censor_time))
}
set.seed(42)
current <- simulate_followup(60, mean_event = 10, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
historical <- simulate_followup(100, mean_event = 11, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  source = c("Current", "Historical"),
  participants = c(nrow(current), nrow(historical)),
  events = c(sum(current$status), sum(historical$status)),
  censored = c(sum(current$status == 0), sum(historical$status == 0))
))
```

```{r survival-fits}
set.seed(42)
current_only <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = TRUE, alpha_max = 0)
set.seed(42)
discounted <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1)
set.seed(42)
full_borrowing <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
  data = current, data0 = historical, breaks = c(3, 6, 12), surv_time = 6,
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = TRUE, alpha_max = 1)
fits <- list("Current only" = current_only, "Discounted" = discounted,
  "Full borrowing" = full_borrowing)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(fit) {
  arm <- fit$posterior_treatment
  c(alpha = arm$alpha_discount, median = median(arm$posterior_survival),
    lower = unname(quantile(arm$posterior_survival, 0.025)),
    upper = unname(quantile(arm$posterior_survival, 0.975)))
}))
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Historical weight", "Median S(6)", "Lower 95% CrI", "Upper 95% CrI"))
```

The estimated historical weight is `r round(discounted$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, 4)`. The augmented posterior median six-month survival is `r round(median(discounted$posterior_treatment$posterior_survival), 4)`. These summarize survival probability at six months, not median survival time. The full-borrowing result includes the extra baseline-prior contribution described below and should not be called an ordinary pooled analysis.

```{r survival-curves, fig.cap="Posterior median survival curves for the estimated-borrowing fit. These are model-based curves, not Kaplan–Meier estimates; uncertainty is summarized in the six-month table.", fig.alt="Posterior median survival curves for the estimated-borrowing fit. These are model-based curves, not Kaplan–Meier estimates; uncertainty is summarized in the six-month table."}
plot(discounted, type = "survival", print = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Follow-up (months)")
```

# Two-arm example

Add independent current and historical controls with mean event time 12 months, using the same censoring mechanism. All four sources are present.

```{r two-arm-survival}
set.seed(101)
control <- simulate_followup(60, mean_event = 12, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
control0 <- simulate_followup(100, mean_event = 12, mean_censor = 18, horizon = 18)
current_two <- rbind(transform(current, treatment = 1), transform(control, treatment = 0))
historical_two <- rbind(transform(historical, treatment = 1), transform(control0, treatment = 0))
set.seed(42)
fit_two <- bdpsurvival(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment,
  data = current_two, data0 = historical_two, breaks = c(3, 6, 12),
  a0 = 0.1, b0 = 0.1, method = "fixed", fix_alpha = FALSE, alpha_max = 1)
log_hr <- as.numeric(fit_two$final$posterior_loghazard)
knitr::kable(rbind(
  "Log hazard ratio" = quantile(log_hr, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  "Hazard ratio" = quantile(exp(log_hr), c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
), digits = 4)
```

The treatment and control historical weights are `r round(fit_two$posterior_treatment$alpha_discount, 4)` and `r round(fit_two$posterior_control$alpha_discount, 4)`, respectively. The median hazard ratio is `r round(median(exp(log_hr)), 4)`. For an adverse event, a hazard ratio below 1 favours treatment; the corresponding no-effect value on the log scale is zero. The two rows transform both the estimates and credible limits consistently.

```{r hazard-ratio, fig.cap="Posterior hazard ratio from the approximate common-effect calculation. The dashed line marks a hazard ratio of 1.", fig.alt="Posterior hazard ratio from the approximate common-effect calculation. The dashed line marks a hazard ratio of 1."}
ggplot(data.frame(hazard_ratio = exp(log_hr)), aes(hazard_ratio)) +
  geom_density(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "#666666") +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = "Hazard ratio (treatment / control)", y = "Density")
```

# Piecewise exponential model

Partition follow-up at $0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_J=\infty$. For the event-counting convention used when splitting records, interval $j$ is $(\tau_{j-1},\tau_j]$. Let $d_{ij}$ indicate an event in that interval and $t_{ij}$ be exposure *within* the interval, not total follow-up. Define $D_j=\sum_i d_{ij}$ and $T_j=\sum_i t_{ij}$.

The hazard is constant at $\lambda_j$ in interval $j$. Independent Gamma priors with shape $a_0$ and rate $b_0$ give

$$
\lambda_j\mid D_j,T_j\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_0+D_j,b_0+T_j).
$$

The defaults are $a_0=b_0=0.1$. This prior is not flat. The rate parameter has exposure-time units, so a change from months to days requires a corresponding change in $b_0$ to preserve the same prior information.

Let $\ell_j(t)=\max\{0,\min(t,\tau_j)-\tau_{j-1}\}$ be the length of interval $j$ before $t$. Then

$$
S(t)=\exp\left\{-\sum_j\lambda_j\ell_j(t)\right\}.
$$

`ppexp(t, hazards, cuts = c(0, breaks))` returns $1-S(t)$ for each row of hazard draws. Survival probabilities are obtained as one minus that result.

## Fixed borrowing comparison

For one arm, compute $q=\Pr\{S(t^*)>S_0(t^*)\mid\text{data}\}$ from the separate current and historical hazard draws, then $p=2\min(q,1-q)$ and $\alpha=\alpha_{\max}W(p)$. The horizon $t^*$ can therefore change the weight, even though that weight is applied to all intervals. With `fix_alpha = TRUE`, the current one-arm implementation reports the untransformed directional $q$ in `p_hat`; the prescribed weight itself is unaffected. This inconsistency is part of issue 16.

For two arms, compare current and historical hazards separately within treatment and within control. For each such comparison, form interval log hazard ratios, estimate their variances across draws, and combine them using inverse-variance weights. The directional probability of a positive combined log hazard ratio is then transformed to $p=2\min(q,1-q)$. This is not the probability that two continuous parameters are unequal.

The draw-specific survival formulas are not presented as a valid alternative here because the current implementation's standardization, repeated transformation, and interval weighting remain unresolved in issue 16.

## Implemented historical augmentation

For a fixed weight, the current implementation generates augmented hazards as

$$
\lambda_j\mid\text{data},\alpha\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(
(1+\alpha)a_0+D_j+\alpha D_{0j},
(1+\alpha)b_0+T_j+\alpha T_{0j}\right).
$$

It discounts the historical posterior parameters, including their baseline-prior terms. A historical-likelihood power update would instead include $a_0,b_0$ only once [@haddad2017]. The intended construction is under review in issue 17. This distinction matters most when event counts or exposure are small, or the prior is influential. In two arms, the implementation uses separate treatment and control weights in this same update.

## Approximate two-arm effect

From the augmented arm hazards, calculate for each draw

$$
R_j^{(s)}=\log\lambda_{jT}^{(s)}-\log\lambda_{jC}^{(s)},
\qquad V_j=\operatorname{Var}_s(R_j^{(s)}),
$$

and combine intervals as

$$
\beta^{(s)}=\frac{\sum_j R_j^{(s)}/V_j}{\sum_j1/V_j}.
$$

This is the implemented inverse-variance approximation to a common log hazard ratio. It is not an exact joint posterior fit of a proportional-hazards Poisson regression. A common treatment effect across intervals is needed for a common-hazard-ratio interpretation; with time-varying effects it is a precision-weighted summary. Large-event approximations such as $1/D_{jT}+1/D_{jC}$ do not describe the implemented empirical variances exactly and are unsuitable when an interval has no events.

# Assumptions and sensitivity

Assume independent participants and censoring independent of the event process within each modeled group. Use the same event definition, time origin, and time units across studies. Inspect follow-up support at the chosen horizon; extrapolation beyond observed follow-up depends on the piecewise hazard assumptions.

Check sensitivity to interval boundaries, survival horizon, Gamma priors, discount function, and maximum weight. Sparse or zero-event intervals can be strongly prior-dependent. Compare the interval-specific effects before interpreting a common hazard ratio. The outstanding issues above must be resolved and the complete procedure evaluated before treating these examples as validation of a trial design.
